criteria.description: Correctly names both effects: reward collection (exploitation) and information collection (exploration).
Gives a correct, concrete scenario showing pure exploitation getting permanently stuck due to early noise.

commonErrors: Only naming the effects abstractly without a concrete scenario showing the failure mode.

solutions.fullSolution: Choosing an arm both collects reward now (exploitation) and collects information about that arm for future decisions (exploration). Concrete failure: if arm A happens to give a lucky high reward on its first try while arm B (actually better on average) gives an unlucky low reward on its first try, pure exploitation (always play argmax hat-mu_a) would lock onto A forever, since hat-mu_A stays higher than hat-mu_B from that point on, and B is never tried again to discover its true (better) average. This permanent lock-in based on early noise is exactly the failure mode that motivates tracking a confidence interval (UCB1) rather than just the point estimate.

criteria.description: Correctly explains that the GP definition itself guarantees joint Gaussianity of any finite set of function values (plus noise).
Correctly explains why sigma_0^2 adds only to the diagonal (independent noise across data points, doesn't affect cross-covariances).

solutions.fullSolution:
(a) By definition, a GP specifies that for ANY finite collection of input points, the corresponding function values are jointly Gaussian. So (f(x), f(x_1),..,f(x_n)) is jointly Gaussian by construction. Adding independent Gaussian observation noise to each f(x_i) to get y_i preserves joint Gaussianity (sums of jointly Gaussian and independent Gaussian variables remain jointly Gaussian).
(b) y_i = f(x_i) + noise_i, with noise_i independent across i and independent of f. Cov(y_i,y_i) = Cov(f(x_i),f(x_i)) + Var(noise_i) = k(x_i,x_i) + sigma_0^2 (the noise variance only affects the diagonal, since noise_i is independent of noise_j for i!=j and independent of f, so it contributes nothing to the off-diagonal covariances k(x_i,x_j)). This is exactly why (K+sigma_0^2*I) replaces plain K: it's the covariance matrix of the observed (noisy) y's, not the noise-free f's.

criteria.description: Correctly explains MPI's blind spot: ignores magnitude of improvement, only its probability.
Correctly explains EI's fix: weights probability by improvement size.
Correctly explains beta's role in UCB's explore/exploit balance.

solutions.fullSolution: MPI only cares about the PROBABILITY of exceeding y*, treating a tiny improvement and a huge improvement identically as long as their probabilities of occurring are equal. So MPI can prefer a point offering a high probability of a negligible improvement over a point offering a lower probability of a massive improvement, generally the wrong choice for finding the true global optimum. EI fixes this by weighting the probability of improvement by the SIZE of the improvement (y*-y), so a low-probability-huge-improvement point can beat a high-probability-tiny-improvement point when it should. For UCB, increasing beta up-weights the uncertainty term sigma_D(x) relative to the mean mu_D(x), pushing the policy toward more exploration (favoring uncertain/unexplored regions); decreasing beta favors exploitation (regions already believed good), the same explore/exploit dial as UCB1's beta in the bandit setting.
